title: Ohio and Michigan Went to War and the Only Wound Was a Penknife #history #shorts
description:
In 1835, Ohio and the Michigan Territory both claimed the Toledo Strip, the land around Toledo near the mouth of the Maumee River. Both sides called out the militia, and the only blood of the whole "war" came from a penknife.

Facts used: Michigan's acting governor, Stevens T. Mason, was 23 for most of 1835; Ohio's governor was Robert Lucas. At Phillips Corners in April 1835, Michigan men caught an Ohio survey party and fired shots (accounts differ on whether they aimed over their heads); nobody was hurt and nine surveyors were arrested. In July 1835, Monroe County deputy sheriff Joseph Wood was stabbed with a penknife by Two Stickney (his brother was named One) during an attempted arrest in Toledo; the wound was minor. In 1836 Congress offered Michigan statehood if it gave up the strip, adding the western Upper Peninsula. A convention rejected the deal in September 1836; the "Frostbitten Convention" accepted it on Dec. 14, 1836. Copper was reported in the Upper Peninsula in the early 1840s, and Michigan led the nation in copper from 1847 to 1887.

The scenes are an animated dramatization.
